items.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
items.description: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation?

items.title: ALMA resolves the gravitational reach of a black hole in the early universe
items.description: Astronomers using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) measured the mass of a supermassive black hole in WISE J224607.56−052634.9, also known as W2246-0526. Its light has been stretched by the expansion of the universe to about 5.6 times its original wavelength. This shift, called redshift, tells astronomers that we see the galaxy as it was when the universe was about 1.3 billion years old.

items.title: Super El Niño could leave South Africa short of grazing. Timing of livestock fodder crops is crucial
items.description: South Africa is entering a potentially difficult summer for farmers. El Niño is already established: the warming of the Pacific Ocean's surface that affects weather patterns globally and brings about severe weather phenomena like floods, droughts and heat waves. The World Meteorological Organisation expects it to strengthen into a very strong event toward the end of 2026, with effects likely to continue into early 2027.

items.title: Two transcription factors reproduce the beneficial side of a 'Jekyll and Hyde' viral protein
items.description: LMP1 is an Epstein-Barr virus protein that has a "Mr. Hyde" side that can promote cancer and a "Dr. Jekyll" side that can spur antitumor immune responses. Scientists at Hiroshima University have now traced key antitumor immune effects of LMP1 to two transcription factors, Spi-B and IRF1, and found that expressing the two together made tumor cells easier for the immune system to recognize and better able to activate CD8+ T cells without using the viral protein itself.

items.title: Ancient height trends show technological advances did not always improve living standards
items.description: New research from the University of Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena gives valuable clues as to economic development in various regions across thousands of years. Researchers evaluated 18,457 skeletal remains and analyzed changes in height, estimated from thighbone length. The bones come from 45 different countries across Europe and Asia. The study has been published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

items.title: Written in sand: How dunes reveal the secrets of planetary winds
items.description: Stanford University researchers have shown that the median sand grain size in dunes on Earth and Mars reveals the speed of the winds that formed those dunes. The finding enables scientists to use sand as a wind speedometer for both modern and ancient dunes found across the solar system.

items.description: A Korean research team has identified how impurities interfere with the use of waste plastic pyrolysis oil as a petrochemical feedstock through catalytic experiments and artificial intelligence (AI)-based computational chemistry. items.title: Elusive optical effect paves the way for advanced lidar and nanophotonic technologies
items.description: An international research team, led by scientists from Skoltech, has experimentally demonstrated for the first time the photonic spin Hall shift for light scattered off an optically small particle. This work, published in the Advanced Photonics journal, overcomes a long-standing challenge in optics and could contribute to the development of next-generation optical technologies, advanced radar and lidar systems.

items.title: Study of juries' decision-making addresses disagreement among jurors
items.description: A new study shows that understanding decisions made by juries requires attention not only to their final verdicts but also to how jurors make decisions individually and work together to reach a verdict, especially when they disagree. Led by Tova Cohen, a Ph.D. student at Rutgers School of Criminal Justice, the research studied 35 participants in seven virtual mock juries to examine individuals' characteristics, deliberative participation, changed verdicts and dissent.
